tweet.text:
TL;DR
Last week my agent team burned 36% of my Max 20x weekly limit in less than 20 hours. At that pace the whole week’s allowance would be gone in about 55 hours.

I’d assumed the culprit was context size, since my agents ran until 95% before compacting. The real drain turned out to be cache expiration on idle agents, then paying to re-hydrate their context when they woke up.

I fixed this by making two changes to how I run the team:

- Agents are now ephemeral
- Agents use Beads to do their work

The original agent team
My project used the typical agent orchestrator pattern with eight agents; all running Opus 5.5.

A primary agent runs around the clock and spins up teammates when there’s work, so sometimes the whole team is busy and sometimes it’s just one or two. All of them run until they hit about 95% of their context window, then compact.

After watching the team hemorrhage tokens I asked Claude to estimate how long it would take to exhaust the weekly limit on Pro, Max 5x, and Max 20x.

Simulating exhaustion
Anthropic doesn’t publish weekly caps, so I started with third-party numbers. A blog post from Wokey had some relevant info: For the week of Oct 12 to 19 they put Pro at about $170 a week in API-dollar terms (474 accounts) and Max 20x at about $1,643 (17 accounts).

I had Claude build a Monte Carlo model, 20,000 simulated weeks per scenario, with the things that drive token burn as variables: how many agents are busy each hour, turns per hour, input and output per turn, context window size, and how often the primary wakes up to a cold cache.

The model said Max 20x would last somewhere between 2.7 and 4.5 days (Max 5x about 1.4 to 2.5, Pro well under one). The spread came down almost entirely to one unknown: whether re-reading cached context counts against a subscription limit at all. My agents’ traffic is about 98% cache reads, so that one question moved the answer by a lot.

What Anthropic says about cache reads
Cache reads for Opus 5.5 cost $0.20 per million tokens. What isn’t published is how much a cache read counts against a subscription limit. The usage limits help page says cached content “counts less against your limits when reused,” and that if a cache expires, your next message “counts that content in full again.” Wokey’s measurements estimate a cache-read token uses “close to none” of a plan’s limit.

Based on this, the Monte Carlo model estimated that Max 20x should last up to 4.5 days.

But my Claude usage showed that 36% was gone in under 20 hours; this is 1.8% an hour, which empties the tank in about 2.3 days. Huh?

It turned out that my simulation was wrong because I only included the primary agent’s cache while idle, not the teammate agents.

The logs
Claude Code keeps every session as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects, and each assistant message carries its token usage: uncached input, output, cache reads, and cache writes.

I had Claude sum the previous 20 hours, counting each request once, and pricing at Opus 5.5 API rates (this is hand-wavy since my plan isn’t billed per token, but API prices are the only ones published).

The third row in the table is the most interesting. For my purposes I defined a rebuild as a request that writes at least 100K tokens to cache after more than 5 minutes of silence from the same agent. Claude found 72 of them in the logs, every one from an agent teammate (not the primary), with each rewriting roughly 490K tokens of context.

If cache reads really are close to free, rebuilds ate about half of everything that counted against my limit.

Why idle is expensive
It turns out that the default idle time for a primary agent in a Claude Code session is 1 hour but subagents and spawned agents default to 5 minutes, source.

The way this plays out in practice is that when an agent teammate finishes a chunk of work and waits on the primary or a teammate for >5 minutes, its cache is cleared. Then it costs $5 per million tokens to rewrite. Then the agent does more work, which adds to the context, and that goes stale and needs to be rebuilt.

Live and learn
I changed two things about my setup that have helped:

1. Ephemeral agents

Teammates don’t wait around anymore so cache rebuilds have been largely removed as a variable. The primary spawns an agent for one task, the agent does the work and exits, and the next task gets a fresh agent.

This design introduces another problem in that new agents don’t know anything about the project. The fix is to add a way for the agents to get relevant context.

2. Beads

Beads is an issue tracker built for coding agents by Steve Yegge. Each bead is an issue with a description, acceptance criteria, notes, and links to the issues it depends on. When the primary agent hands out work, the agent gets one issue.

That does two things: The context an agent carries is sized to its task and the state of the work lives in the tracker instead of in an agent’s context window. This also helps if an agent dies unexpectedly; the next agent just picks up the issue where the last left off.

I’ve used Beads religiously for over a year but intentionally left it out of this project just to see how good modern Claude Code agents were.

It turns out that today’s agents run into many of the same communication and coordination problems that existed when Steve originally wrote Beads. So, yeah, it’s really an essential tool for agentic engineering.

A couple of other settings that can help are to configure spawned agents to have a 1-hour cache (docs) and compact earlier than 95%, so a rebuild rewrites less.

Do it yourself
If you run agent teams on a plan, you can do this check yourself. Point Claude at ~/.claude/projects, ask it to sum cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, and output_tokens per hour, and look for big cache writes that follow a gap of more than five minutes. It takes only a few minutes.
